sentences.text: Pachyornis is an extinct genus of flightless ratites from New Zealand belonging to the moa family.
This bird had a sternum lacking a keel, a trait shared by all ratites.
Three species of Pachyornis are currently recognized: P. geranoides, P. elephantopus, and P. australis.
P. elephantopus is considered the species with the most extreme morphology within the genus Pachyornis.
The animal resembled eastern moa or broad-billed moa but was distinguished by a pointed bill and a heavier build.
It also possessed a distinctive palate structure.
The genus Pachyornis was first described by Richard Lydekker in 1891.
There are 24 recorded fossil occurrences of Pachyornis in the Paleobiology Database.
Pachyornis species went extinct after human colonization of New Zealand, though P. australis may have died out earlier.
Pachyornis geranoides is the type species of the genus Pachyornis.
The parent group of the genus Pachyornis is the family Emeidae, which is part of the broader moa family.
Two distinct genetic lineages found in the North and South Islands suggest the genus might eventually be expanded to five species.
Pachyornis lived from the Gelasian epoch to the Holocene, spanning 2.58 to 0 million years ago, though fossils are recorded only from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene.
Fossils of Pachyornis date from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene.
